abstract: The brain of modern humans has evolved remarkable computational abilities enabling higher cognitive functions. Recent progress in evolutionary genomics and experimental neuroscience has identified several human-specific genetic modifiers of brain development that underlie the emergence of human-specific traits of cortical circuit connectivity and function. The human-specific gene SRGAP2C emerged by partial duplication of the ancestral gene SRGAP2A, which encodes a postsynaptic protein regulating synaptic development. SRGAP2C inhibits all known functions of SRGAP2A and its expression in mouse cortical pyramidal neurons leads to neotenic synaptic maturation, increased cortico-cortical connectivity, increased reliability of sensory coding by cortical layer 2/3 PNs, and improved learning of a sensory discrimination task. However, it remains unclear whether SRGAP2C expression in the mouse cortex is sufficient to produce changes in cognition. To test this idea, we trained adult wild-type (WT) and SRGAP2C mice on a Go-NoGo task that involves learning to associate a whisker stimulus with the presence of a water reward. SRGAP2C mice displayed a licking strategy that accelerated the learning of stimulus-reward associations at the cost of punishment timeouts compared to WT mice. The licking strategy was selective to the task, not driven by a general increase in consumptive behavior, and it accelerated the information that SRGAP2C mice gathered in early learning. SRGAP2C mice also displayed more structured behavior later in training and were, overall, better information channels than their WT counterparts. A computational model confirmed that SRGAP2C mice learning strategy increases representational capacity. Our results reveal that expression of human-specific gene SRGAP2C in cortical circuits is sufficient to increase the cognitive abilities of mice by optimizing the use of sensory information to guide action. The human-specific gene SRGAP2C might have contributed to the emergence of distinct functional cortical circuit features underlying our unique learning abilities and flexible decision-making.
